statements.feedback: Clean — active voice and indicative mood from start to finish.
statements.text: The coach blew the whistle, and the players ran to the sidelines.

statements.feedback: Trap: the first half is active (The students built), then the verb goes passive (was abandoned) with no signal. Keep the voice the same unless the shift is deliberate.
statements.text: The students built the float, and then it was abandoned by everyone for two weeks.

statements.feedback: Deliberate shift for effect — a command dropped in after a statement, clearly marked by 'Do not' alone. That's a writer's choice, not an accident.
statements.text: This meeting has been going for ninety minutes. Do not raise your hand until we reach the final item.

statements.feedback: Statement flips to command mid-sentence with no signal. Readers trip because 'please sit down' arrives like it belongs to the movie.
statements.text: The movie ends at nine, so please sit down quietly and leave before the credits finish

statements.feedback: Passive voice here is on purpose: the machine (not the person) is the point, and the passive keeps the subject consistent.
statements.text: The new door is opened by a sensor, and it is closed again automatically after ten seconds.

statements.feedback: The subject drops out and the tone snaps from formal to casual mid-paragraph — an unmarked shift readers have to decode.
statements.text: Applicants must submit their forms by Friday. Also, don't forget to actually, like, sign the thing, guys.

data.summaryBody: The fix rule is the same every time: keep voice and mood consistent unless the shift is clearly marked as intentional. Passive voice and commands are not errors by themselves — sneaky, unmarked changes are.

blocks.purpose: Choose the only correct fix among tempting flawed rewrites, confronting the common error of thinking any passive voice or any command is automatically wrong.

options.text: Every sentence should avoid the passive voice completely, so rewrite it as 'The relay team finished the race, and the victory was celebrated by everyone.'
options.whyNot: Tempting, but this makes the second half passive with no reason. Passive is not automatically wrong — an unmarked shift is.

options.text: Keep the voice the same: 'The relay team won the race, and the whole school celebrated the victory.'
options.whyNot: This one survives: one subject focus, active voice all the way through, and no surprise switch for the reader to decode.

options.text: Break the mood up on purpose: 'The relay team won the race. Celebrate the victory!'
options.whyNot: Nothing in the original signals a deliberate shift to a command, so this invents a mood change the writer never marked.

options.text: The second half is a fragment, so just delete it: 'The relay team won the race.'
options.whyNot: The second half has its own subject and verb, so it is not a fragment — deleting good content solves nothing.

data.prompt: A sports section reads: 'The relay team won the race, and the victory was celebrated by the whole school.' Which fix is actually correct?

blocks.purpose: Mixed grid combining rhetorical grammar (end-focus, fronting, parallel structure) with voice/mood patterns, preventing the two topics from blurring together.

cells.answer: The subject does the action (The chef chopped onions).
cells.feedback: Active keeps the doer up front, which usually reads faster and stronger.

cells.answer: The subject receives the action (The onions were chopped by the chef).
cells.feedback: Passive is a legitimate tool when the receiver matters more than the doer.

cells.answer: Statements and questions of fact (She studies every night. Does she study?)
cells.feedback: Indicative is the default mood — the ordinary 'this is happening' mode.
The subject 'you' is understood and usually left out — that's your cue for imperative.

cells.answer: Wishes, demands, or conditions contrary to fact (I suggest that she study every night.)
cells.feedback: Watch for that-clauses after verbs like suggest, demand, insist — the subjunctive drops the normal -s.

cells.answer: End-focus: the reader remembers the last words best, so the news lands last (Stolen from the vault, overnight, was the crown itself.)
cells.feedback: Word order is a rhetorical tool: what comes last gets the weight.
acceptedAnswers: the end of the sentence carries the emphasis
save the key information for last

cells.answer: Build suspense: hold the main clause until the end, then release it (After three flat tires, a wrong turn, and a dead phone, we finally reached camp.)
cells.feedback: Periodic = point comes last. Cumulative = its mirror image.
acceptedAnswers: withholds the main clause until the end

cells.answer: Lead with the main clause, then pile on detail (We finally reached camp, after three flat tires, a wrong turn, and a dead phone.)
cells.feedback: Cumulative front-loads the point and accumulates texture after it.

data.decisionPrompt: Write the new announcement: two sentences maximum, one consistent voice and mood, with one deliberate rhetorical pattern that makes the 7:30 deadline feel urgent.

misconception.detail: You kept the passive voice or mixed a command into statements without marking it. The fix: pick one voice (active) and one mood (imperative works for a directive), and let the parallel phrases carry the emphasis — that's the rhetorical layer doing the persuasive work.
misconception.title: Voice drifted, or the pattern never appeared

data.rationalePlaceholder: Name the voice, the mood, and the rhetorical pattern you chose — and why...
data.referenceNote: You may lean on one line of notes: 'Consistent voice and mood unless the shift is intentional; deliberate patterns carry persuasion.'

rule.name: Consistent voice and mood, plus one deliberate pattern
rule.statement: Keep the voice and the mood consistent unless the shift is clearly intentional, and use a rhetorical pattern (parallel structure, periodic order, or cumulative detail) so the sentence persuades, not just reports.

data.scenarioBody: Your class is running the annual museum field trip, and last year's announcement confused everyone. The draft above mixes a statement, a passive construction, a command, and casual slang — and nobody knew what they actually had to do. The principal wants a new announcement of at most two sentences that (1) keeps one voice and one mood throughout, and (2) uses one deliberate rhetorical pattern from rhetorical grammar — a periodic build-up, a cumulative detail pile, or a parallel structure — to make the deadline feel urgent. The facts students need: the bus leaves at 7:30 a.m. sharp, students should pack a lunch, bring a signed permission slip, and arrive ten minutes early.

targetAnswer.decision: Students: before 7:30 a.m. on trip day, pack a lunch, sign your permission slip, and arrive ten minutes early — because the bus leaves at 7:30 sharp, and it will not wait.
targetAnswer.rationale: I kept the voice active throughout (students pack, sign, arrive; the bus leaves) and the mood consistent (imperative-style directive wrapped in indicative statements), so there is no unmarked shift. The parallel list 'pack a lunch, sign your permission slip, and arrive ten minutes early' builds rhythm and makes the demands feel official, and end-focus puts the urgent fact — the bus will not wait — in the last position, where readers remember it.

checks.prompt: Which statement best defines voice in grammar?
checks.answer: Whether the subject performs the action or receives it
checks.rationale: Voice is specifically about whether the subject acts (active) or is acted upon (passive) — tone and time are different features.
checks.hint: Ask: who is doing the action, and where does that doer sit in the sentence?
choices: Whether the subject performs the action or receives it
Whether the verb is in the past, present, or future
Whether the tone is formal or informal
Whether the sentence states a fact or gives a command
checks.focus: Recall definitions of voice and verb moods with no cues

checks.prompt: A draft reads: 'The scouts sold the cookies, and the racks were emptied by the customers in an hour.' What is the best fix for the unmarked voice shift?
checks.answer: Keep the second half active: 'The scouts sold the cookies, and the customers emptied the racks in an hour.'
checks.rationale: The sentence opens in active voice and slips into passive mid-sentence with no signal, so the fix restores consistent active voice.
checks.hint: Look at who the doer is in each half of the sentence.
choices: Keep the second half active: 'The scouts sold the cookies, and the customers emptied the racks in an hour.'
Change the first half to passive: 'The cookies were sold by the scouts, and the customers emptied the racks in an hour.'
Keep it as is, since passive voice is always the more formal choice
Split it into a fragment: 'The scouts sold the cookies. Emptied by the customers.'
checks.focus: Identify and fix an inappropriate active-to-passive shift mid-sentence

checks.prompt: In a paragraph of deliberate one-word fragments and punchy sentences, a writer suddenly drops in 'The novel was praised by the critic' where the surrounding sentences are all active. In one word, which voice did this sentence shift into?
checks.rationale: Surrounding sentences keep the subject as doer; this one makes the subject the receiver of the action, which is the passive voice.
checks.hint: Which voice hides the doer behind 'by the critic'?
checks.focus: Distinguish careless shift errors from deliberate fragments in a paragraph

checks.prompt: A memo says: 'Form must be turned in by Friday, so turn it in, ok?' Which rewrite keeps voice and mood consistent throughout?
checks.answer: 'Turn in your form by Friday, and the office will file it that day.'
checks.rationale: Only the first option holds one consistent voice and mood across both halves without an unmarked change.
checks.hint: One mood, one voice — and no casual tag-ons.
choices: 'Turn in your form by Friday, and the office will file it that day.'
'You must turn in your form by Friday, and the form is filed by the office that day.'
'Turn in your form by Friday, and your form should really be turned in, okay?'
'Turn in your form by Friday! File your form today!'
checks.focus: Choose the rewrite that keeps voice and mood consistent

checks.prompt: A sentence opens with a string of details — 'After two lost keys, a wrong bus, and a locked gym door — ' and saves its main clause, 'the assembly finally started,' for the very end. Which structure is this?
checks.rationale: Holding the main clause until the end is the definition of a periodic sentence; cumulative does the reverse.
checks.hint: Where does the main clause land — first or last?
checks.focus: Match rhetorical structures (periodic, fronting, parallel) to their effects across mixed topics
